contentHtml:
A well-designed pooja room sits in the northeast of the home where possible, with the deity facing east or west so you face east or north while praying. In apartments, a wall-mounted or floor-standing mandir unit with a jali or glass shutter works best; in villas, a dedicated room is ideal. Use calm materials like marble, solid wood or Corian, warm concealed lighting, a heat-safe diya ledge, and closed storage for pooja essentials.

For many families in Gurgaon, the pooja room is the one part of the home that isn't negotiable. It's often the first thing parents ask about when a new flat is being planned, and the last thing anyone wants to get wrong.

The challenge is that modern homes rarely come with one. Builder floor plans in new towers on Dwarka Expressway, Sohna Road and Golf Course Extension Road usually leave the mandir for the homeowner to fit in, while villas and independent floors in DLF phases and Sushant Lok have more room but need careful planning to feel special rather than tucked away.

This guide covers pooja room design ideas that work in real Gurgaon homes: Vastu-friendly placement, layouts for apartments and villas, materials, lighting, storage and safety.

Where Should the Pooja Room Be? Vastu Placement Basics

Vastu Shastra is a traditional guide, and families follow it to different degrees. These are the placement principles most commonly followed, and the ones we plan around when a client asks for a Vastu-compliant mandir.

Vastu principleWhat it means in practice
Best directionNortheast (Ishan kona) of the home; east or north are the usual alternatives
Direction you faceFace east or north while praying, so the deities face west or south
Height of idolsIdols placed around chest height of the person praying, never directly on the floor
Idol sizeSmall idols are generally preferred; many practitioners suggest under about 9 inches
AvoidUnder a staircase, next to or sharing a wall with a toilet, and inside a bedroom where possible
ColoursLight, calm tones such as white, cream, pale yellow or light wood

If your apartment's northeast corner is a bathroom or balcony, don't worry. Most families choose the best available option (usually an east or north wall in the living or dining area) and many consult their own Vastu expert or family elder before finalising.

Pooja Room Design Ideas for Apartments

In a 2BHK or 3BHK flat, the mandir usually has to share space with the living or dining area. The goal is to give it a sense of its own place without taking up a room.

OptionTypical footprintBest for
Wall-mounted mandirAround 2–3 ft wide, 12–15 in deepCompact 2BHKs; keeps the floor clear
Floor-standing mandir unitAround 2.5–4 ft wide with base storage3BHKs; gives drawers for pooja items
Corner mandir with partitionA 3×3 to 4×4 ft corner screened by jali or glassLiving-dining areas with a spare corner
Wall niche or alcoveRecessed into a wall or built between columnsHomes where a shallow recess exists
Converted store or utility nookSmall room of about 3×4 ft or moreHomes with an unused store near the living area

For apartments, closed shutters are practical. Glass or CNC jali doors keep dust and pets out, let light glow through and allow you to close the mandir when you have guests. If you are designing the whole flat, our 2BHK layout guide shows how to plan the living-dining zone so the mandir wall stays uncluttered.

Pooja Room Design Ideas for Villas and Large Homes

Villas, independent floors and 4BHK+ apartments can usually give the mandir a dedicated room. That opens up design possibilities apartments don't have.

  • Dedicated pooja room: a small room with a raised platform for the deities, space to sit on the floor for aarti, and a door you can close.
  • Double-height or skylit mandir: in villas with volume, a tall mandir wall or a skylight above brings natural light onto the deities.
  • Courtyard-facing mandir: placing the pooja room beside a garden or courtyard creates a calm transition into the space.
  • Family gathering space: leave enough floor area for the family to sit together during festivals, typically in front of the mandir rather than beside it.

For larger homes, the pooja room often becomes part of a wider layout plan. See how we approach this in our 4BHK layout guide and 5BHK space planning guide.

Materials for a Modern Pooja Room

MaterialLook and feelThings to know
White marbleClassic, serene, traditionalDurable and heat-resistant; can be carved or inlaid
Solid wood (teak, sheesham)Warm, traditional, rich grainNeeds polishing; keep flames away from exposed wood
Veneer on plywoodWood look at a lower weightPair with a stone or metal ledge where diyas are lit
Corian / solid surfaceSeamless, modern, can be backlitCNC-carvable; heat tolerance depends on the product, so use a stone diya ledge
CNC jali (wood, MDF, metal)Patterned screens with shadow playPopular for doors and back panels; choose moisture-resistant boards
Brass and copper accentsFestive, traditional warmthBells, handles and trims; polish periodically
Backlit onyx or stoneLuxurious glowPremium option for villas and statement walls

For eight more design styles, from backlit marble to concealed pocket-door mandirs, see our guide to mandir design for home.

Pooja Room Door and Back Panel Ideas

  • Glass doors with etched motifs: Om, lotus or bell patterns keep the mandir visible but protected.
  • CNC jali doors: geometric or temple-inspired patterns in wood or metal, lit from behind for depth.
  • Bells on the door frame: small brass bells add sound and ritual without extra space.
  • Backlit back panel: a jali, onyx or Corian panel with warm LED behind it creates a soft halo around the deities.
  • Temple-arch frame: a subtle arch or stepped frame gives a traditional silhouette to an otherwise modern unit.

Lighting, Storage and Safety

Lighting

Use warm light (around 2,700 K) so the brass, marble and flowers glow rather than look flat. Concealed LED strips behind a jali or along the top shelf, a small spotlight on the main deity, and a separate switch for the mandir are usually enough. Many families add a warm electric diya for everyday use and keep oil diyas for pooja time.

Storage

Plan closed drawers for incense, matchboxes, cotton wicks, oil, prayer books, bells and festival décor. A shallow drawer just under the idol platform keeps daily items within reach, while deeper base drawers store thalis and seasonal items. A pull-out drawer for a floor aasan or folding stool is useful in apartments.

Safety

  • Give diyas a stone or metal ledge, never bare wood, veneer or fabric.
  • Keep curtains, garlands and paper décor clear of the flame zone.
  • Allow ventilation for incense smoke, especially in closed pooja rooms. A small exhaust or jali opening helps.
  • Keep the smoke detector position in mind when you plan where agarbatti and dhoop will burn.

Pooja Room Design Dos and Don'ts

DoDon’t
Raise the idol platform off the floorPlace idols directly on the floor
Keep the mandir clean and unclutteredStore unrelated items inside the mandir unit
Use warm, soft lightingUse harsh white downlights over the deities
Plan electrical points before carpentryRun exposed wires or extension boards to the mandir
Use heat-safe surfaces for diyasLight diyas on wood, veneer or laminate
Leave space to sit or stand in frontSqueeze the mandir behind a sofa or door swing

What Affects the Cost of a Pooja Room?

Pooja room cost varies widely because it can be anything from a compact wall unit to a carved marble room. The main factors are size and type (wall unit, floor unit or full room), material (laminate and veneer at one end, carved marble, onyx and solid teak at the other), craft work such as CNC jali, inlay or hand carving, lighting and backlighting, and any civil work to create a niche or room. When a mandir is planned as part of a full home interior, it is designed and executed alongside the rest of the carpentry, which usually keeps the finish consistent and the process simpler. For full-home budgets, see our 2BHK, 3BHK & 4BHK interior design cost guide.

How The Omega Group Designs Pooja Rooms

We treat the mandir as a piece of custom furniture with a very specific brief: the direction your family prefers, how you pray (standing or seated), how many people gather during festivals, and which idols and items it must hold. We then design it in 3D alongside the rest of your home, fabricate it with our custom furniture team, and install it with the same 70+ quality checks we use across every project.

faqs.question: Which direction is best for a pooja room as per Vastu?
faqs.answer: The northeast of the home is considered best for a pooja room in Vastu, with east and north as common alternatives. While praying, you should ideally face east or north.

faqs.question: Can I have a pooja room in a small apartment?
faqs.answer: Yes. A wall-mounted mandir around 2 to 3 ft wide, a floor-standing unit with storage, or a screened corner in the living-dining area all work well in compact 2BHK and 3BHK flats.

faqs.question: Can the mandir be placed in the bedroom?
faqs.answer: Vastu generally advises against a bedroom mandir. If there is no other option, place it in the northeast corner of the bedroom with doors or a curtain that can be closed at night.

faqs.question: What is the best material for a pooja room?
faqs.answer: White marble and solid wood are the most traditional choices. For a modern look, Corian, veneer and CNC jali panels work well, as long as diyas sit on a stone or metal ledge.

faqs.question: At what height should idols be placed in a mandir?
faqs.answer: Idols are usually placed around chest height of the person praying, so decide first whether your family prays standing or seated. Idols should never sit directly on the floor.

faqs.question: Can the pooja room share a wall with a bathroom?
faqs.answer: Vastu advises against sharing a wall with a toilet or bathroom. If it cannot be avoided in an apartment, choose a different wall or leave a gap with a storage unit between the two.

faqs.question: What colours are best for a pooja room?
faqs.answer: Light, calm colours such as white, cream, pale yellow and light wood tones are most commonly used, with brass or gold accents for warmth.
